analysis.one_liner: Caps mandatory nurse overtime at 48 hours a week at Medicare providers, with whistleblower protections.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate's final month with no cosponsors, the bill never left the Finance Committee and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made Medicare providers, as a condition of participating in Medicare, stop requiring nurses to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, more than 12 consecutive hours, or during the 10 hours right after a 12-hour shift. Time spent on call would count as work time. It would let nurses report violations, protect them from retaliation, and let federal officials fine repeat violators up to $10,000 per knowing violation. Exceptions would apply only during declared emergencies, and states with stronger rules would keep them.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses at hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare providers, who could no longer be forced past 48 hours a week or into back-to-back shifts without real rest. Their patients benefit too, because the bill's findings cite research linking nurse fatigue to medical errors even after accounting for staffing levels.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits providers from requiring nurses to work beyond a scheduled shift, more than 48 hours in a workweek, more than 12 consecutive hours in a 24-hour period, or during the 10 hours immediately after the 12th hour worked, with on-call and standby time counted as hours worked.

Gives nurses the right to file complaints with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, requires investigation, and bars providers from firing, penalizing, or retaliating against nurses who refuse mandatory overtime or report violations, including retaliatory reports to state licensing boards.
Allows civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, stiffer penalties for patterns of repeated violations, and public posting of penalized providers' names and violations.

Exempts providers only during declared emergencies, and only after reasonable efforts to fill staffing gaps, and explicitly excludes understaffing and labor disputes from counting as emergencies; it also leaves stronger state laws untouched.
Cites research that nurses working long hours experience fatigue and impaired vigilance that contributes to medical errors, and notes 18 states already restrict mandatory nurse overtime.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other Medicare providers, which would need to hire enough nurses to cover shifts without mandatory overtime or limit how many patients they accept, and could face fines for violations.

drawbacks.text: Ending a nurse's shift mid-episode of care means handing the patient to someone new, and the bill's own findings acknowledge potential pitfalls of discontinuity in care from limiting work hours.

Because consistent understaffing does not qualify for the emergency exception, providers with chronic vacancies would have to hire more staff or reduce capacity, a real cost for rural and small facilities that already struggle to recruit nurses.
Penalty records are removed from the public HHS website one year after a change in ownership, weakening accountability for corporate-owned facilities that are sold.
Voluntary overtime remains fully allowed, so nurses under financial pressure could still end up working the long hours the bill aims to prevent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a clear, enforceable limit on a practice the bill's findings link to nurse burnout and medical errors, backed by real penalties and whistleblower protection. The costs fall on hospitals and clinics, chiefly the expense of staffing shifts without relying on forced overtime, and handoff discontinuity is a genuine but manageable trade-off that 18 states have already accepted. The ownership-change carve-out on penalty records is a real weakness. On balance the protections outweigh the costs, though the bill never got far enough for the trade-offs to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate's final month with no cosponsors, referred to the Finance Committee, and sat there until the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, never receiving a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on December 1, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No cosponsors joined, and no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have tied nurse overtime limits to Medicare participation, covering hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, critical access hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, home health agencies, rural health clinics, and federally qualified health centers.

It included an exception for declared emergencies with staffing-effort conditions, whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections, posting and documentation requirements, and civil money penalties up to $10,000 per knowing violation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and other Medicare providers came out ahead, since they can keep using mandatory overtime to cover shifts and understaffing without facing federal penalties, and nurses gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that rely on mandatory overtime

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon and the bill's only sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 1, 2022, in the closing month of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no senator cosponsored, so the bill's support never grew past its single Democratic sponsor and the partisan shape cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from requiring nurses past 48 hours a week or 12 consecutive hours, forcing them to hire sufficient staff instead, and exposed repeat violators to $10,000 fines and public penalty records. Their preference for staffing flexibility came at the expense of nurses' rest and patient safety.

With mandatory overtime off the table, hospitals facing a sudden vacancy would have had to fill shifts through alternative means, which typically means hiring agency staff at premium rates. That eases the burden on nurses but adds cost to hospitals that may flow to patients and insurers.
